name: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence: Key Readings
description:
To what extent may phenomenology contribute to a better understanding of the basic concepts, presuppositions, and aims of AI? One of phenomenology’s main contributions to science in general (i.e., not only with respect to AI), is to clarify the basic concepts and statements of the respective field of investigation. It does so not by providing explicit definitions, but by explaining these basic concepts and statements in a way that does not amount to a reduction to some indefinable concepts. The phenomenological approach, as Gödel once put it with respect to Husserl’s method, is a way of “focusing more sharply on the concept concerned by directing our attention […] onto our own acts in the use of these concepts, onto our powers in carrying out our acts, […]. [It is] a procedure or technique that should produce in us a new state of consciousness in which we describe in detail the basic concepts we use in our thought, or grasp other basic concepts hitherto unknown to us”.
On which assumptions is the AI’s conception of the mind as an information-processing system based? Is intentionality an exclusivity of minds, or could a suitably programmed computer also be able to exhibit intentionality? Can the mind and all phenomena associated with it be reduced to a set of mechanical transformations or computations? Based on the discussion of various classical works from the field of philosophy of artificial intelligence (e.g., Dreyfus, Turing, Searle, among others), this course aims at shedding light to these and other fundamental philosophical questions concerning the relationship between AI and the human mind from a phenomenological perspective.
